title: GOD CALLED IT UNCLEAN—BUT DID HE EVER CALL THE WOMAN WORTHLESS?
paragraphs: GOD CALLED IT UNCLEAN—BUT DID HE EVER CALL THE WOMAN WORTHLESS?
Why Leviticus Forbade Sex During Menstruation—and How One Misunderstood Law Has Left Generations of Women Carrying Shame God Never Placed on Them
There is a kind of shame that never announces itself.
It enters quietly.
Through a careless sermon. Through a Bible verse taken out of context. Through a religious tradition repeated so often that nobody thinks to question whether it actually reflects the heart of God.
And sometimes, it enters through something as ordinary as a woman's monthly period.

Imagine being told that something your body does naturally makes you spiritually disgusting. That your blood makes you undesirable. That your husband should avoid you because God supposedly sees something wrong with you.
Now imagine opening your Bible and discovering these words:
“Also thou shalt not approach unto a woman to uncover her nakedness, as long as she is put apart for her uncleanness.” — Leviticus 18:19 (KJV)
And then, only two chapters later, discovering an even more frightening warning:

“And if a man shall lie with a woman having her sickness, and shall uncover her nakedness; he hath discovered her fountain, and she hath uncovered the fountain of her blood: and both of them shall be cut off from among their people.” — Leviticus 20:18 (KJV)
Both of them?
Cut off?
For having sexual intercourse during menstruation?
Why would the God who created the female body establish such a severe prohibition concerning a normal biological process?
Was menstruation considered sinful?
Was the woman somehow less holy?
Was God punishing her for being female?
And perhaps the most important question of all:
If Jesus Christ has fulfilled the Law, what are Christians supposed to do with these verses today?

Stay with this, because the answer requires us to walk through ancient Israel, understand the Hebrew Scriptures, confront a deeply rooted confusion about holiness, and finally stand before Jesus Christ Himself.
And when we get there, something extraordinary becomes clear.
The God who established boundaries concerning ritual impurity is the same God who welcomed a bleeding woman when everyone else had reason to keep their distance.
That is not a contradiction.
That is a story of holiness, fulfillment, and grace.
And it deserves to be understood correctly.
Before we can understand why Leviticus prohibited intercourse during menstruation, we must understand something many modern readers overlook.
In the Old Testament, being ritually unclean was not automatically the same as being morally sinful.
That distinction changes everything.
The Hebrew word commonly translated as “unclean” is טָמֵא (ṭāmēʾ).
It describes a condition of ritual impurity within Israel's ceremonial system.
It does not inherently mean wicked, immoral, disgusting, rejected, or personally worthless.
This is crucial because Scripture describes several situations that could result in ritual impurity.
Contact with a dead body could make someone unclean (Numbers 19:11).
Certain bodily discharges could make someone unclean (Leviticus 15).
Childbirth involved a period of ritual purification (Leviticus 12).
Even a man experiencing a normal emission of semen became ceremonially unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:16–18).
Think about that last example.
A man could become ritually unclean through a normal bodily function.
And a woman could become ritually unclean through a normal bodily function.
Neither condition, by itself, meant that the person had committed a moral offense.
The distinction was not between valuable people and worthless people.
It was between ritual states that mattered within Israel's covenant worship.
The Hebrew Bible also uses the word קָדוֹשׁ (qādôš), meaning “holy,” associated with being set apart or consecrated to God.
Ancient Israel was called to be holy because the Lord Himself was holy.
“Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy.” — Leviticus 19:2 (KJV)
God's holiness shaped Israel's worship, daily practices, relationships, and boundaries.
And the ceremonial laws taught Israel to recognize distinctions between what was clean and unclean, holy and common.
But those distinctions should never be carelessly transformed into declarations about a person's human dignity.
A woman experiencing menstruation was not suddenly less human.
She had not lost the image of God.
She had not become an inferior member of creation.
She was experiencing a bodily process within a covenant community whose worship was governed by particular laws of purity.
Ritual impurity described a condition under the Law. It was not a measurement of someone's worth before God.
And this is where the story becomes more complicated.
Because Leviticus did not merely say that menstruation resulted in temporary impurity.
It specifically prohibited sexual intercourse during that time.
Why?
To understand that prohibition, we need to look closely at the Hebrew text.
Leviticus 18:19 says:
וְאֶל־אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ לֹא תִקְרַב לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ
Ve'el-ishshah beniddat tum'atah lo tiqrav legalot ervatah.
A careful rendering is:
“And you shall not approach a woman during the impurity of her menstruation to uncover her nakedness.”
The expression לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה (legalot ʿervah) literally concerns “uncovering nakedness.”
Within Leviticus 18, this is a conventional expression referring to prohibited sexual relations.
The word נִדָּה (niddāh) is associated here with menstruation and the corresponding state of ritual impurity.
So the prohibition is not a command forbidding a woman from being touched, spoken to, respected, loved, or cared for.
The immediate subject is sexual intercourse.
That matters.
Because when Scripture gives a specific prohibition, we must resist the temptation to expand it into accusations Scripture itself does not make.
God did not say, “A menstruating woman is worthless.”
He did not say, “Her husband must stop loving her.”
He did not say, “Her body is disgusting.”
The law addressed a particular sexual act during a particular ritual condition.
And Leviticus 20:18 treated a deliberate violation of that prohibition as a serious covenant offense.
Notice something else.
The penalty addressed both the man and the woman.
The text did not place responsibility solely upon the woman because she was menstruating.
It concerned their participation in the prohibited act.
This distinction is essential.
The woman's menstrual condition was not itself the offense. The prohibited sexual intercourse was.
Now we must ask the harder question.
Why did the Law treat this act so seriously?
The Bible does not provide a single sentence explaining every reason behind this particular command.
So we must be careful.
Some interpreters emphasize the ceremonial significance of blood.
Others emphasize the preservation of boundaries surrounding sexuality and bodily discharges.
Others observe that Leviticus 18 places this prohibition among laws governing sexual conduct within Israel's covenant community.
These observations can illuminate the context, but we should not pretend that Scripture explicitly supplies a complete medical, symbolic, or social explanation.
What Scripture does clearly reveal is that blood carried profound significance within Israel's sacrificial system.
Leviticus 17:11 declares:
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.”
In Hebrew, the opening words include:
כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הַבָּשָׂר בַּדָּם הִוא
Ki nefesh habbasar baddam hi.
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood.”
Here, נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh) carries the sense of life or living being.
Blood was not treated casually in Israel's worship because God had assigned it a special role in atonement.
But we must not confuse the sacrificial use of blood with the specific rules about menstruation.
Menstrual blood was not itself sacrificial blood, and Leviticus does not explicitly say that menstrual intercourse was forbidden because menstrual blood was intended for atonement.
The connection is broader: blood, bodily states, life, death, and holiness all mattered within Israel's ritual world.
The menstrual laws belonged to that world.
They were not simply ancient medical advice.
And they should not be defended by claiming that intercourse during menstruation is inherently poisonous, medically dangerous, or universally harmful.
Scripture does not make those claims.

Modern medical considerations are a separate matter. Menstrual intercourse is not inherently unsafe, although sexually transmitted infections, pregnancy possibility, comfort, consent, and individual health circumstances remain relevant.
We honor Scripture more faithfully when we explain what it actually says instead of inventing scientific arguments to make an ancient command sound persuasive.
But perhaps you're still wondering:
Why would a loving God establish such strict boundaries in the first place?
Because the Law was never intended to teach Israel that God was ordinary.
His presence was holy.
His covenant was serious.
And approaching Him was not something His people could define entirely on their own terms.
Leviticus repeatedly reminds Israel that holiness involves distinction.
The people were learning that they belonged to the Lord.
Their worship, their bodies, and their conduct were not disconnected from that calling.
Yet here is the tragedy.
A law intended to govern holiness can become an instrument of humiliation when people confuse ceremonial status with human value.
And history has shown how easily religious language can be used to wound.
A woman hears the word “unclean” and begins to believe she is dirty.
A young girl experiences her first period and feels ashamed of a body she never chose.
A wife wonders whether her husband sees her as less desirable.
A believer quietly asks whether God is disappointed in something He Himself designed.
If that is you, please hear this carefully.
Your menstrual cycle is not proof that God despises your body.
You do not need to repent for menstruating.
You do not need to apologize for being female.
You do not need to earn back a dignity that your Creator never took away.
Genesis 1:27 declares:
“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.”
Male and female.
Both created in God's image.
Both possessing human dignity.
Both accountable to God.
Both in need of His grace.
And both able to receive salvation through Jesus Christ.
But the story does not end in Leviticus.
Because centuries later, another woman appears in Scripture.
A woman whose life had been marked by blood.
Not for seven days.
Not for a single monthly cycle.
But for twelve exhausting years.
Her story is recorded in Mark 5:25–34.
And it may be one of the most emotionally powerful encounters in the Gospels.
Picture her.
Twelve years of bleeding.
Twelve years of searching for relief.
Twelve years of disappointment.
The Bible tells us she had suffered greatly under many physicians, spent everything she possessed, and grown worse rather than better.
Her body was exhausted.
Her resources were gone.
Her hope had been battered.
And under the purity regulations of Leviticus 15:25–27, her prolonged bleeding would have had serious ritual implications.
We should not invent every detail of her social life, because Mark does not tell us precisely how her family or community treated her.
But the weight of her condition is unmistakable.
She had suffered for years.
And then she heard about Jesus.
Maybe she heard that He healed the sick.
Maybe she heard that He welcomed people others overlooked.
Maybe she heard enough to believe that one encounter could change what twelve years of suffering had not.
Mark 5:27–28 says:
“When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment. For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole.”
Imagine that moment.
The crowd pressing around Him.
People reaching.
Voices calling.
Dust rising beneath their feet.
And somewhere among them, a suffering woman carrying twelve years of desperation.
She reaches out.
Her fingers touch His clothing.
And immediately, the bleeding stops.
But the most beautiful part of the story is not simply that her body was healed.
It is what Jesus did next.
He stopped.
He asked who had touched Him.
The woman came forward, trembling, and told Him the truth.
And Jesus said:
“Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.” — Mark 5:34 (KJV)
Daughter.
Let that word settle into your heart.
Not “disgusting.”
Not “worthless.”
Not “unwanted.”
Daughter.
The Greek word is θυγάτηρ (thygatēr).
Daughter.
A personal, relational form of address.
Jesus did not treat her suffering as evidence that she had lost her dignity.
He received her, healed her, and sent her away in peace.
And the Greek word translated “peace” is εἰρήνη (eirēnē).
It carries the sense of peace and well-being.
She came seeking healing.
She left having heard the voice of Jesus call her “Daughter.”
Do not misunderstand this scene.
Mark does not explicitly say Jesus was conducting a debate about Leviticus 18:19 or repealing that particular sexual prohibition.
The woman had a prolonged flow of blood; the passage concerns her healing, not sexual intercourse during menstruation.
And the story should not be used to claim that Jesus simply considered God's earlier laws foolish.
That is not what the Gospel teaches.
But it does reveal something profoundly important.
Jesus did not regard a suffering woman's ritual condition as a reason to deny her mercy.
Her condition did not make her invisible to Him.
Her desperation did not offend His compassion.
Her trembling confession did not make Him turn away.
And her encounter with Him points us toward something greater.
The fulfillment of God's redemptive purposes in Jesus Christ.
This is where we must understand the difference between ancient Israel's covenant laws and the Christian's life under the New Covenant.
Jesus declared:
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.” — Matthew 5:17 (KJV)
He did not come to announce that holiness no longer mattered.
He came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets.
His sinless life, sacrificial death, and resurrection stand at the center of that fulfillment.
Hebrews explains that the old covenant's sacrificial and ceremonial arrangements pointed toward greater realities accomplished through Christ.
Hebrews 9:13–14 contrasts outward ceremonial purification with the cleansing of the conscience through the blood of Jesus.
And Hebrews 10:1 describes the Law as having a shadow of the good things to come.
The New Testament does not command Gentile Christians to maintain Israel's entire ritual purity system.
Acts 15 records the early church wrestling with what should be required of Gentile believers.
The apostles did not impose the whole Mosaic Law upon them.
At the same time, they did call believers to abstain from sexual immorality.
That distinction matters because Christians should not assume that every Old Testament sexual prohibition was merely ceremonial or that every rule operates identically under the New Covenant.
We must read each passage carefully in the light of Christ and the teaching of His apostles.
The New Testament does not explicitly repeat Leviticus 18:19 as a binding menstrual-intercourse prohibition for Christians.
Christians differ in how they apply this Old Testament command today, particularly across traditions that understand continuity with Mosaic sexual laws differently.
But there is no clear New Testament basis for declaring that a Christian woman becomes spiritually contaminated simply because she menstruates.
Nor should someone be told that menstruation separates her from the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Our acceptance before God does not rest upon maintaining Israel's ceremonial purity regulations.
It rests upon Jesus Christ.
His sacrifice.
His righteousness.
His grace.
And His finished work.
Listen to Hebrews 10:22:
“Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.”
The invitation is to draw near.
Not because our bodies never bleed.
Not because we have never experienced weakness.
Not because we have perfectly navigated every question about the Law.
But because Jesus Christ has opened the way.
And perhaps this is where the conversation becomes personal.
Because menstrual shame is only one form of shame people carry into their relationship with God.
Some people feel unclean because of something their bodies do.
Others feel unclean because of something they have done.
A secret addiction.
An affair.
A lie.
A betrayal.
A sexual history they cannot undo.
A marriage they damaged.
A decision they regret.
A hidden sin they keep promising to abandon.
And this is where we must distinguish two truths that should never be separated.
A natural bodily function is not a moral sin. But actual sin is real, and it calls for repentance.
The Gospel does not tell us that sin is imaginary.
It tells us that forgiveness is possible.
It does not call evil good.
It calls sinners to turn toward the Savior.
It does not erase holiness.
It reveals the Holy One who gave Himself to redeem us.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice the difference.
A woman does not need forgiveness for menstruating.
A sinner needs forgiveness for sin.
And every one of us, male or female, needs the grace of Jesus Christ.
That is why the cross matters.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die because human bodies were inherently disgusting.
He died for our sins.
He bore the judgment we deserved.
He gave Himself to reconcile sinners to God.
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin and death would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
There is a reason our message at Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same truth:
Not because Jesus pretends our past never happened.
Not because He calls sin harmless.
Not because He promises that every painful consequence will disappear overnight.
But because the risen Christ can redeem people whose stories appear beyond repair.
He can forgive the guilty.
He can restore the repentant.
He can receive the ashamed.
He can strengthen the exhausted.
And He can teach us to stop calling people worthless when God has made them in His image.
Maybe you are a woman who grew up believing your body was something to apologize for.
Maybe you are a husband who has never considered how carelessly spoken words about purity could wound your wife.
Maybe you are a parent teaching a daughter about menstruation and wondering how to explain the Bible without creating fear.
Maybe you are a pastor who has preached these passages but never stopped to distinguish ritual impurity from moral guilt.
Or maybe you are someone who has used Scripture to condemn another person without first taking the time to understand what God actually said.
There is grace for the repentant heart.
And there is responsibility for those who teach.
Because Scripture is not ours to manipulate.
It is not a weapon for humiliating people.
It is God's Word, and we are accountable for how faithfully we handle it.
Second Timothy 2:15 calls believers to rightly handle the word of truth.
That means studying context.
It means understanding covenant history.
It means refusing convenient interpretations that the text cannot support.
And it means allowing Jesus Christ to remain at the center of our understanding.
So what should a Christian husband and wife do today regarding intercourse during menstruation?
They should approach the question with biblical seriousness, mutual respect, honesty, and consideration.
Neither spouse should use Leviticus to degrade the other.
Neither should use grace as an excuse for coercion or selfishness.
First Corinthians 7:3–5 emphasizes mutual marital responsibilities and agreement concerning periods of abstinence.
Christian intimacy should never become an occasion for pressure, humiliation, or disregard for another person's well-being.
A couple may choose to abstain during menstruation for reasons of conviction, comfort, health, or personal preference.
Another couple may understand the Old Testament ritual prohibition as no longer binding under the New Covenant.
Whatever their conclusion, it should not be built upon the false belief that a menstruating woman has lost her worth before God.
Love does not require the humiliation of the beloved.
And holiness does not give anyone permission to be cruel.
The same Jesus who taught the seriousness of sexual purity also showed extraordinary compassion toward people who were suffering.
We need both truths.
Truth without compassion can become harsh and distorted.
Compassion without truth can become sentimental and misleading.
But in Jesus Christ, we see holiness and mercy together.
John 1:14 describes Him as full of grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Grace and truth.
And perhaps that is what some of us have been missing.
We have been so busy defending our interpretations that we have forgotten the people listening.
The girl who thinks God hates her body.
The woman who believes her normal biology makes her spiritually inferior.
The husband who is confused about how to honor Scripture and love his wife.
The believer who is frightened by the severity of an Old Testament penalty.
The seeker who wonders whether the Bible offers dignity or only condemnation.
They deserve more than a careless answer.
They deserve Scripture explained faithfully.
They deserve the distinction between ritual impurity and moral sin.
They deserve to hear about the fulfillment of the Law in Christ.
And they deserve to know that the Gospel is not an invitation to despise the human body, but a call to redemption through the One who took on human flesh.
Jesus Christ did not come to make us ashamed of being human. He came to save us from sin and reconcile us to God.
And now I want to ask you something.
Not for an argument.
Not for a performance.
But for an honest conversation.
Have you ever heard a Bible verse explained in a way that made you feel rejected by God, only to discover later that its context told a different story?
Have you ever carried shame that Scripture never actually placed upon you?
Or have you ever realized that something you taught others about God needed to be corrected?
And if this helped you distinguish biblical holiness from unnecessary shame, tell us what changed in your understanding.
Your testimony or question may help another person who has been too afraid to speak.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that they are not alone in seeking understanding.
Not to start a fight.
Not to embarrass anyone.
But to help the truth reach someone who needs it.
Invite your family, your friends, those struggling with faith, and even those who are not yet believers to join us.
Because discipleship is not about winning arguments.
It is about knowing Christ, understanding His Word, and being transformed by His truth.
And that brings me to something close to the heart of this ministry.
Every article we publish, every Scripture we explain, every difficult question we examine, and every resource we make available is part of a larger mission.
To help people move from confusion to biblical understanding.
From spiritual exhaustion to renewed hope.
From hidden sin to repentance.
From shame to grace.
And ultimately, from separation from God to reconciliation through Jesus Christ.
These resources are offered to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and continue their discipleship beyond a single Facebook post.
But continuing and expanding a ministry requires time, work, resources, and faithful support.
Not because God's grace is for sale.
It isn't.
And not because supporting this particular ministry is a requirement for glorifying God.
It is not.
We glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to us.
One way you can express that generosity is by helping sustain Gospel Warrior.
But we want to be clear about an important biblical distinction.
Scripture teaches that giving should come from a willing heart.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not grudgingly.
Not under pressure.
Not because someone frightened you into believing God would reject you if you did not pay.
But freely, prayerfully, and joyfully.
Those products can serve as reminders of faith, tools for study, and opportunities to share encouraging messages with others.
It is the opportunity to help make Scripture-centered teaching and free Christian resources available to more people.
Sometimes the person who needs a message most is not the person who follows the ministry.
It is the friend who sees it because you shared it.
The family member who has stopped attending church.
The believer who is quietly questioning everything.
The woman who has spent years thinking her body makes her unacceptable before God.
Or the person who has confused the shame of being human with the conviction of actual sin.
One faithful share can open a conversation.
One thoughtful comment can encourage someone to study.
One testimony can remind another believer that grace is real.
And one person turning to Jesus Christ is worth far more than any number on a screen.
Because the goal has never been simply to build an audience.
The goal is to point people toward the Savior.
And as we return to the question that began this article, perhaps we can now answer it with greater clarity.
Why did Leviticus forbid intercourse during menstruation?
Because ancient Israel lived under a covenant in which ritual purity, bodily conditions, sexual boundaries, and the holiness of God's presence were regulated by specific divine commands.
The prohibition was real.
The covenant consequences were serious.
But the woman's menstruation was not itself a moral offense, and ritual impurity did not mean she was personally worthless.
In Jesus Christ, Christians encounter the fulfillment of the Law and the promise of cleansing that reaches deeper than outward ceremonial conditions.
The Gospel calls us to repent of real sin, receive God's grace through faith, and walk in holiness.
It does not require us to invent shame where Scripture has not placed it.
And if you remember nothing else from this article, remember the woman in the crowd.
Twelve years of suffering.
One desperate reach.
One encounter with Jesus.
And one word that still echoes through the centuries.
Daughter.
That is what He called her.
Not because her suffering was imaginary.
Not because the Law had never mattered.
But because the mercy and authority of Jesus Christ were greater than the despair she carried.
So if you have been made to feel worthless because of something God designed your body to do, do not confuse another person's misunderstanding with God's judgment.
And if you are carrying genuine guilt because of sin, do not confuse repentance with hopelessness.
Come to Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn away from what needs to change.
Receive the forgiveness He offers.
And learn to walk in the freedom of His truth.
Because the cross does not teach us that holiness is unnecessary.
It teaches us just how costly our redemption was.
And the empty tomb declares that our past does not have to possess the final word.
The woman who feared her blood made her untouchable reached for Jesus—and discovered that His mercy was never beyond her reach.
